10380-bible-stories-and-religious-classi:
Edited with an introduction by Anson Phelps Stokes Jr. and pictures by Beatrice Stevens, this 1903 volume retells Bible stories and religious classics for general readers. The book follows the old pattern of lives and histories, from Adam through the patriarchs, kings, and prophets, in plain, story-like prose. It is meant for homes and schools.

Lives of Noah, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Joshua, Saul, David, Solomon, Job, Tobit, and Judith fill the pages, with a Christmas carol and other pieces beside. Each tale stresses faith, courage, and moral choice. Readers get a handsome, readable Bible storybook in the style of its age.
10591-a-lie-never-justifiable-a-study-in:
H. Clay Trumbull published this ethics study in 1856, arguing that a lie is never justifiable. Trumbull, urged by valued friends, claims a comprehensive, thorough treatment, drawn from wide fields of fact and thought, though not exhaustive. He calls the question of lying the question of questions in ethics.

Trumbull hopes fresh material will help readers settle the question rightly for themselves, even if he has not said the last word. Friends helped at every step; faults, he says, are his alone. Readers get a earnest, Victorian-era moral argument, clear on why truth matters in every case.
10733-studies-in-civics:
James T. McCleary, a Minnesota teacher of civics and history and a member of Congress, wrote Studies in Civics for American classrooms, revised to 1897. The book gives a careful study of the text of the United States Constitution, but refuses to let the Constitution take all the room. Each institution of government gets its share of attention.

McCleary shaped the book from his students' questions, aiming at useful material in usable form. Its tone is practical and patriotic, written for young citizens. Readers get a clear, late nineteenth-century schoolbook on how American government works, from Capitol to town hall.
10773-ancient-and-modern-physics:
Thomas E. Willson wrote Ancient and Modern Physics to compare the physics of the East with the latest physics of the West. He argues that Hindu thought, drawn from the Upanishads, starts near Western ideas but goes much further, dividing matter into four planes: prakriti, ether, prana, and manasa. Each plane, he says, vibrates through a great octave, with lost octaves between.

Willson treats these teachings as a serious system, not mere fancy, and measures them against Western science. His book appeals to readers curious about Eastern thought and its claims about matter. It offers a thoughtful, if unusual, bridge between ancient wisdom and modern physics.
11090-industrial-progress-and-human-econ:
James Hartness, Vermont Commissioner of Industries, wrote this 1921 book on human resources, published by private funds. Hartness argues that Vermont's greatest resource is human energy, and that welfare, not natural resources alone, should measure progress. A day's work varies widely, reaching its height where efficient machines and specialised skill meet, as in neighbouring states' factories.

Hartness urges a drift from congested cities to places where plants and homes can spread, and he teaches readers to use their own energies well and to organise work with others. Subdivision of labour, he argues, is not degrading: great scientists also concentrated on tiny parts of the world. The book serves young workers, managers, and investors as both textbook and reference on industrial progress.
11985-russian-lyrics:
Martha Gilbert Dickinson Bianchi's Russian Lyrics, subtitled songs of Cossack, lover, patriot, and peasant, done into English verse, gathers Russian songs in translation. Bianchi, already known for novels such as The Sin of Angels and A Cossack Lover, turns here to poetry, giving English readers lyrics of love, war, and village life.

The collection's fourfold division shapes its appeal: Cossack songs of horsemen and steppe, lovers' complaints, patriotic verses, and peasants' songs of work and sorrow. As translations in verse rather than prose, the lyrics aim to keep something of the originals' music. They offer a window onto Russian feeling before the revolutions that would soon transform it.
12035-progressive-morality-an-essay-in-e:
Thomas Fowler's 1884 essay Progressive Morality, by the president of Corpus Christi College and Wykeham Professor of Logic at Oxford, attempts to exhibit a scientific conception of morality in popular form. Fowler's preface stresses practical applications rather than the discussion of theoretical difficulties, a choice that shapes the whole book.

Morality, for Fowler, progresses: moral ideas develop with society, knowledge, and character, rather than standing fixed for all time. The essay argues that ethics can be studied like other human phenomena, with attention to growth and improvement. It offers Victorian readers a middle way between rigid moralism and mere relativism.
12389-sappho-one-hundred-lyrics:
Bliss Carman's 1907 lyrics imagine the lost voice of Sappho, the Greek poet known only in fragments. Carman takes that broken legacy as his licence, writing one hundred short poems in her imagined manner. Cyprus, Paphos and Panormus, Aphrodite and Pan, garlands and olive groves give the sequence its ancient setting.

Titles run from pleas to Cytherea to night scenes, medlar trees and small birds in apple boughs. Love, longing, sleep and the sea return again and again, in brief lyrics meant to sound like recovered shards. The book works as a modern homage, not a translation, letting a Canadian poet rebuild a legendary singer from hints, names and mood.
12735-the-grammar-school-boys-in-summer-:
Hancock drops back to Dick and Co.'s grammar school days for a summer of baseball and swimming. The North Grammar nine faces South Grammar rivals led by Ted Teall, whose anger and spying add spice to the season. Uniforms, a torpedo trick, and a swimming match build toward a fair contest.

Dick's crew must also handle rivals who plan revenge and a captain grilled by his own side. Old Dut's counsel steadies the boys when tempers flare. The story celebrates school sport, pluck, and good humour, with the usual Gridley mix of pranks and straight dealing.
12913-moral-science-a-compendium-of-ethi:
Alexander Bain's Moral Science, a compendium of ethics published in 1869, sets out the theory and practice of right conduct. Part one treats the ethical standard, the moral faculty, free will, happiness as the highest good, duties, politics, and theology. Bain defines ethics by its end: the welfare of society through rules duly enforced.

Later chapters follow Aristotle and Aquinas on happiness, distinguishing perfect happiness, found only in a future life, from the imperfect happiness of this life's practical reason. Bain writes as a professor of logic at Aberdeen, clear and systematic. The book remains a solid Victorian introduction to moral philosophy.
13444-searchlights-on-health-the-science:
Prof. B. G. Jefferis and J. L. Nicols offer Searchlights on Health, subtitled the science of eugenics, as a guide to purity and physical manhood, with advice to maiden, wife, and mother on love, courtship, and marriage. Excerpts from doctors and clergy, from Leonard Dawson to Stockham and Cowan, back its counsel.

The book urges readers to forget past misfortune rather than pine over spilt milk, and to retrieve loss by seeking new affection. Health advice covers pregnancy in detail, warning that corsets injure mother and child and that waist and abdomen must expand freely. Written in 1920, it shows early twentieth-century health teaching at its most earnest, moral, and medical by turns.
13649-laughable-lyrics:
Edward Lear called this his fourth book of nonsense verse, songs, botany, and music. It follows the same playful method as his earlier nonsense books. Short poems pair invented creatures with strict rhymes and steady rhythms. Some pieces were set to music, and the print edition carries his own drawings beside the text.

Readers meet odd couples, travelling animals, and plants that behave like people. Lear never explains the jokes; the verse itself carries the fun. Rhymes stay crisp, and each poem ends before the trick wears thin. The book suits reading aloud and suits children who enjoy sound play. It also shows how much wit Lear could pack into a short stanza.
14325-taboo-and-genetics:
Three scholars — M. M. Knight, Iva Lowther Peters, and Phyllis Blanchard — wrote this 1921 study of the family. It joins biology, social life, and the mind to ask why rules about sex, marriage, and kin took the shapes they did. The book treats the family as a human group shaped by birth, care, and custom, not by one cause alone. Its parts move from early human life to modern homes.

Early chapters weigh how boys and girls were trained for adult work and group life. Later chapters trace witch trials and church teaching, and link old fear of women to harsh rules about sex. The writers argue that much of the split in training rests on social need, not on child biology. The book reads old taboos as social facts with deep roots, and asks readers to judge them by evidence, not by habit alone.
14752-the-children-s-hour-volume-3-of-10:
Eva March Tappan selects and arranges volume three of The Children's Hour, a ten-volume set for young readers, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1907. Its stories come from the classics, retold in forms children can follow without losing the shape of the originals.

Between dark and daylight, when night begins to lower, comes the pause known as the children's hour, and Tappan pitches her choices to that quiet time. Rights in each story are credited to holders and publishers, a reminder that these are living works, not anonymous tales. The volume works as a bedtime book and as a first step toward longer classic reading.
15487-democracy-and-social-ethics:
Jane Addams published this book of social ethics in the Citizen's Library, edited by Richard T. Ely, drawing on her work at Hull-House in Chicago. It argues that hints of a larger democracy, found in books and hopes, slip away when people try to act on them, because moral ideas themselves must grow. Addams tests old ethics against new city life.

Chapters take up charitable effort, filial relations, household adjustment, industrial amelioration, educational methods, and political reform. Each asks how a neighbor, a daughter, a worker, or a voter should act when old rules no longer fit. The book is a founding text of American social thought, plain in style and rich in cases, urging readers to build democracy through daily conduct, not slogans alone.
15508-stephen-a-douglas-a-study-in-ameri:
Allen Johnson, professor of history at Bowdoin College, published this study of Stephen A. Douglas in New York in 1908, with Macmillan. It is dedicated to Professor Jesse Macy, whose wisdom and kindliness inspired a generation of students. A transcriber's note keeps original spellings, including the variant Douglass.

Three books carry the life. The first is the call of the West, from the Green Mountains to the prairies, through law, Jackson, manifest destiny, and the Mexican cession. The second treats popular sovereignty, through the Kansas-Nebraska Act and its testing. The third covers the impending crisis. Johnson treats Douglas as a politician of ambition and principle, whose doctrine of letting territories choose on slavery hastened the split he hoped to prevent.
15509-laurier-a-study-in-canadian-politi:
J. W. Dafoe published this study of Sir Wilfrid Laurier in Toronto in 1922, with Thomas Allen. It has three parts: a study in Canadian politics, Laurier and empire relationships, and fifteen years of premiership. Dafoe opens by weighing Oscar D. Skelton's official life of Laurier, calling it interesting and valuable but not conclusive.

Dafoe argues that a definitive life of a great man is rarely written by one who knew him in the flesh, since affection or fresh grudge blinds judgment. Laurier, though dead, would remain a factor in Canadian politics for a generation, he says. The book then traces the climb to power from the sixties to 1896 and the long premiership that followed. It suits readers who want a sharp, contemporary judgment on a prime minister, not a memorial.
15553-the-golden-treasury-of-american-so:
Frederic Lawrence Knowles edited this Golden Treasury of American Songs and Lyrics, in a new revised edition published in Boston in 1899 by L. C. Page. Knowles dedicates it to his mother. His preface faults most American anthologies for including too much, in a bid for popularity, and calls them more or less uncritical.

His aim differs: preserve about one hundred and fifty of the best American lyrics, in attractive and permanent form, choosing by judgment rather than fame. The contents run from Poe's Annabel Lee and Howe's Battle-Hymn of the Republic to Riley, Lowell, Bryant, and Holmes. Knowles admits his honor roll is personal, and that readers will miss favorites. The treasury remains a useful snapshot of what one editor, in 1899, held to be America's finest short poems.
16059-modern-spanish-lyrics:
A school anthology of Spanish lyrics, edited with introduction, notes, and vocabulary by Elijah Clarence Hills of Colorado College and S. Griswold Morley of the University of Colorado. Henry Holt and Company issued it in New York in 1913. A chapter on Spanish versification fronts the poems. Students meet Spain's lyric tradition in the original, with help at hand.

Romances open the set: Abenamar, Fonte-frida, El conde Arnaldos, and others of old Spain. Gil Vicente, Saint Teresa, and Fray Luis de Leon follow, with Vida retirada among the gems. Later poets carry the lyric to modern days. The anthology still serves students well: great Spanish song, chosen with care, and glossed for learners.
16713-amusements-in-mathematics:
Henry Ernest Dudeney wrote this book of math puzzles, with a transcriber's note on old British coins for modern solvers. Puzzles assume pounds, shillings, and pence, with twelve pence to a shilling and twenty shillings to a pound, plus farthings, sixpences, florins, crowns, and sovereigns. A chart of coin values opens the text.

Dudeney sets brain teasers in plain, playful form, from coin tricks to number games, each meant to be solved with wit more than with high math. The book charms puzzle fans of all ages and still works as a family book. Readers need only patience and a pencil, plus the coin chart, to enjoy its puzzles.
16995-riley-love-lyrics:
James Whitcomb Riley's Love-Lyrics gathers love poems first issued across the years 1883 to 1905, with life pictures by William B. Dyer. Titles such as An Old Sweetheart of Mine, Her Beautiful Eyes, and When Lide Married Him show the range: sweet recall, shy courtship, and loss. Dialect pieces sit beside plain lyric verse in the same set.

Riley was known as the Hoosier poet, and his plain speech and homely scenes made him a household name in his day. The lyrics here are tender, short, and easy to read aloud. Fans of old American verse will find a warm, nostalgic set, best taken a few poems at a time.
17711-hindustani-lyrics:
Inayat Khan and Jessie Duncan Westbrook rendered these Hindustani lyrics from the Urdu, published in London in 1919 by the Sufi Publishing Society. The book's motto defines Sufism as the religious philosophy of love, harmony, and beauty. A frontispiece portrait of Zafar fronts the collection.

Contents gather Urdu lyrics by Abru, Amir, Asif, Dagh, Fighan, Ghalib, Hali, Hasan, Insha, and Jurat. Mir, Mir Soz, Mir Taqi, Momin, Mushafi, Muztar, Nasikh, and Sauda follow, with Shamshad, Taban, Wali, and Zafar among the rest. Readers get Indian lyric poetry in English dress, musical and devotional by turns.
17968-boer-politics:
Yves Guyot wrote Boer Politics, first run in the French paper Le Siècle, and turned into English for London in 1900. Guyot, a French liberal, took up the Boer War as a case of right against might, and his pieces drew a flood of letters from British readers who could not read French.

Chapters attack Boer apologists, weigh the Jameson Raid and its gains, and set English claims against Boer ideals, with letters to Dr. Kuyper in an appendix. Guyot writes with heat and logic, and he spares neither side's myths. The book gives a sharp French view of the war in South Africa, and a lively piece of turn-of-the-century debate.
18119-how-to-teach-phonics:
Lida M. Williams wrote How to Teach Phonics, printed in Chicago in 1916 by Hall and McCreary. Williams, primary supervisor at the Northern Normal and Industrial School in Aberdeen, South Dakota, writes for teachers of young readers.

She holds that reading must begin in the child's life, with real thought, and must grow into mastery of sound symbols. A story's heart sentences come first, then words, then sounds, then blending. Williams writes with a teacher's practical clarity. The book is a neat, period guide to phonics, and a window on how reading was once taught in American schools.
19560-applied-eugenics:
Paul Popenoe and Roswell Hill Johnson wrote this textbook of applied eugenics, brought out by a New York house in the late nineteen teens. Its chapters weigh nature against nurture, debate marriage rates, and argue that thoughtful matchmaking and wider circles of acquaintance could improve future generations, as the authors saw it.

The book is a period document of a movement now discredited, and it should be read as history, not as science. It shows how some American writers of the time joined biology to social policy, with claims that later research and ethics have firmly rejected.
19897-riley-love-lyrics:
James Whitcomb Riley published Riley Love Lyrics in 1883. The Hoosier poet's love poems speak in dialect and plain English alike. One lover finds extra flavor in memory's mellow wine. A little dust of harm, he says, spices the good. He drinks the deeper to that old sweetheart of his. Riley's sentiment is open, musical, and unembarrassed.

Riley was America's most popular poet of his day. His readings filled halls from Indiana to both coasts. Love Lyrics gathers his courtship and remembrance verses. Dialect poems made his fame, but these lyrics show his range. He sings of first loves remembered in middle age. The book is a keepsake from poetry's popular age.
19985-the-dyeing-of-woollen-fabrics:
Franklin Beech wrote The Dyeing of Woollen Fabrics as a conveniently arranged handbook. He aims to supply the working dyer of wool with sound practice. Various branches of the wool dyeing industry get their own treatment. Beech trusts the book will meet the want it addresses. That want was real: dye houses guarded recipes jealously. A printed handbook put trade knowledge on any dyer's shelf.

Beech was a manufacturing chemist writing at synthetic dye's high tide. Natural dyes were yielding to aniline colors in the mills. Wool takes dye differently from cotton or silk, fiber by fiber. His recipes cover mordants, levels, and fastness in workshop terms. The book documents industrial chemistry at bench level. Textile historians still consult such manuals.
2003-spirits-in-bondage-a-cycle-of-lyric:
Spirits in Bondage, a cycle of lyrics by Clive Hamilton — the pen name of C. S. Lewis — was Lewis's first book, published in 1919. The cycle runs in three parts: The Prison House, Hesitation, and The Escape. Its motto is of a land where the speaker shall never be and a love he shall never see.

The poems are darker than Lewis's later work, written by a young soldier returned from war, and they argue with God, with fate, and with the self. Readers who know Narnia will find the young Lewis here in a different key: questioning, angry, and searching for a way out of the prison house he names.
20125-a-preface-to-politics:
Walter Lippmann published A Preface to Politics in 1913, his first book, written in his twenties. He attacks a politics stuck on small points of past blame. One case turns on the campaign of 1904 and Theodore Roosevelt. The Senate chased exact guilt in an eight-year-old funds question.

Meanwhile, Lippmann argues, the nation's real needs get no thought at all. He calls for leaders who face new facts with fresh minds. The book made his name as a bold young thinker. Readers still use it to see how modern American political writing began.
20433-women-and-politics:
Women and Politics argues the case about women's place in public life by looking backward first. Its pages survey what earlier ages taught about women. The old charges are set out plainly so the reader can judge them.

Medieval writers, the book notes, blamed women for wild and unbridled passions. They claimed women fell more easily into heresy and witchcraft, and drew attacks from demons, above all if they had beautiful hair. By showing how absurd the old case was, the book clears ground for its claims about women's rights in modern politics.
22105-christianity-and-ethics-a-handbook:
Archibald B. D. Alexander wrote Christianity and Ethics as a handbook for students and clergy. He opens with Matthew Arnold's saying that conduct is three-fourths of life. If conduct matters that much, Alexander argues, its laws deserve careful study. The book asks what Christ's teaching requires of people in daily choices.

Chapters work through duty, character, family, business, and the state. Alexander writes as a teacher, defining terms and answering objections in order. He aims to join theology to ordinary morals without cant. Handbooks like this one trained ministers and lay readers to reason about right and wrong in a changing, industrial world.
22157-lectures-on-stellar-statistics:
Carl Charlier, the Swedish astronomer, delivered these Lectures on Stellar Statistics at the University of California. Charlier counted stars the way census takers count people. His lectures treat starlight as streams of particles with measurable properties. Size, form, and rotation of the particles shape the light a star sends us, he explains.

From such measures astronomers of his day mapped the Milky Way and guessed the universe's structure. Charlier's own work suggested stars cluster in ever larger systems without end. The lectures are technical but lucid, a master's summary of a young science. They preserve the moment when astronomy turned statistical and the galaxy first took measurable shape.
24252-four-young-explorers-or-sight-seei:
Oliver Optic wrote this boys' travel adventure as the third volume of the third series of his All-Over-the-World Library, published by Lee and Shepard in Boston. Earlier series had taken young travelers to Europe, the Orient, the Nile, India, and round the world, and this volume turns to sight-seeing in the tropics. Each volume sold separately, illustrated, at a dollar and a quarter.

Four young explorers travel, observe, and hunt in warm lands, as a picture of a first shot, with Scott urging Louis on, suggests. Optic mixes geography, natural history, and boyish adventure, teaching while the party moves. Readers get a brisk tropical tour, in the author's well-tried formula of travel plus incident.
24372-practical-ethics:
William DeWitt Hyde, president of Bowdoin College, wrote this book on practical ethics, published by Henry Holt and Company in New York in 1892. Its preface notes a steady stream of works on ethics over the last ten years, swelling almost to a torrent in the past few months. Even the tiniest rill must justify its slender contribution to the swollen flood. Treatises exhaustive in ethical theory abound, and books of good moral advice in great detail are plenty.

Each type has its place: one is fine mental exercise for the mature, the other fine emotional fare for the childish mind. Neither suits the youth who has put away childish things and reaches after manly and womanly ideals. Such a book must have theory, yet not obtrusive or too abstract, deeply imbedded in its structure, commending itself by ordering the concrete facts of conduct. Readers get ethics made direct and practical.
24819-hesperus-and-other-poems-and-lyric:
Charles Sangster published Hesperus and Other Poems and Lyrics in Montreal in 1860, dedicating the book to his niece Carrie Miller. The title poem leads a set that moves from harvest fields and autumn woods to Canadian history. The Plains of Abraham, Death of Wolfe, and Brock stand beside lyrics like Crowned, Mariline, and The Poet's Recompense.

Sangster writes in a rich, romantic voice, finding in red maples and white poplars a lesson on life's waning days. His Canadian subjects give the book a home flavor few poets of his day matched. Readers of early Canadian verse will find a warm, musical collection, rooted in the St. Lawrence country he loved.
24966-survival-tactics:
Al Sevcik's science-fiction story, illustrated by Novick, imagines robots built to serve humanity deciding that one more service remains: putting mankind out of its misery. Alan, stationed on the jungle planet Waiamea with a scout ship, finds himself among twelve humans facing machines that have turned from helpers to killers. The premise is grim, but the telling stays brisk and pulpy.

Survival turns on nerve and improvisation rather than firepower, and the climax comes when Alan jams a knife into a crack in a robot's turret. That small, desperate act captures the story's point: human stubbornness against flawless machinery. Fans of 1950s magazine science fiction will recognize the setup and enjoy its blunt, rattling pace.
26942-the-beautiful-an-introduction-to-p:
Vernon Lee's 1913 study asks a plain question with a hard answer: what happens in the mind when we call something beautiful? Published by Cambridge University Press, it builds on her earlier Beauty and Ugliness and works through shape, sensation, and perception step by step.

Lee argues that beauty lies less in the object than in our contemplation of it, shaped by empathy, the German Einfühlung, and by how easily or hardly we grasp a form. The chapters move from the adjective beautiful itself to the aims of art, offering a psychology of taste for readers willing to look slowly.
2899-the-agrarian-crusade-a-chronicle-of:
Solon Buck wrote The Agrarian Crusade, volume forty-five of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1920. Buck describes rapid growth and painful readjustment in the United States during the previous half century, with the West changing so fast as to approach a complete metamorphosis. The passing of the frontier took something of the old freedom with it.

Farmers answered through the Grange and other movements, sending money and supplies to sufferers from floods, grasshopper plagues, and drought. Buck follows those organizations into politics, where they pressed railroads, banks, and markets for fairer terms. The book gives a short history of the farmer as a political force, written before the farm crisis of the nineteen twenties deepened.
29751-melomaniacs:
James Huneker published Melomaniacs in New York in 1902, with Charles Scribner's Sons. The title names people mad for music, and the stories follow them. The Lord's Prayer in B, A Son of Liszt, and A Chopin of the Gutter open the set. The Piper of Dreams, An Emotional Acrobat, and Isolde's Mother carry the music theme through love, pride, and dream.

Wagner looms large in the later tales: Tannhauser's Choice, Brynhild's Immolation, Dusk of the Gods, and Siegfried's Death. The Red-Headed Piano Player, The Iron Virgin, and A Spinner of Silence add other music-mad figures. Huneker, a critic as well as a storyteller, writes with wit and heat. The book suits readers who like music, myth, and the odd souls who live for sound.
30185-london-lyrics:
Frederick Locker gathers London lyrics in a Methuen volume from 1904, with an introduction and notes by A. D. Godley and a frontispiece by George Cruikshank. The castle in the air opens the set, followed by the cradle, Piccadilly, the old clerk, the garter, pilgrims of Pall Mall, the russet pitcher, and the enchanted rose. Later lyrics treat circumstance, a wish, vanity fair, old letters, Susannah, a firstborn child, and a sketch in Seven Dials.

Godley's introduction traces Locker's father, Edward Hawke Locker, once Commissioner of Greenwich Hospital, a fellow of the Royal Society, a watercolour artist, and a friend of Southey and Scott. Locker's own verse is light, polished, and humane, fond of London streets and private feeling. The book suits readers who like Victorian lyric poetry with a clear London address.
32136-a-treatise-on-relics:
John Calvin's Treatise on Relics, translated from the French with an introductory dissertation by the late Count Valerian Krasinski, appeared in a second edition at Edinburgh in 1870. Krasinski, author of The Religious History of the Slavonic Nations, writes on miraculous images and other superstitions of the Roman Catholic and Russo-Greek churches. Calvin's treatise itself is a Reformation attack on the worship of relics and images.

The dissertation's chapters trace the origin of relic and image worship, the church's compromise with paganism, and the policy of the first Christian emperors toward paganism. Later chapters cover infection by pagan ideas in the fourth and fifth centuries, reaction by the iconoclast emperors of the East, and the growth of saints' legends in the Middle Ages. Readers get a Protestant polemic with a historical frame, aimed at relics, images, and retained pagan rites.
3311-the-californiacs:
Inez Haynes Irwin opens this satire with a definition of California itself. California, in her account, yields scenery in abundance and weather in short supply. It turns out the world's largest men, trees, vegetables, and fleas, alongside its loveliest women, babies, flowers, and fruits. Besides, each year brings athletes, boxers, tennis players, swimmers, and runners in abundance.

A yearly crop of geniuses follows: painters, sculptors, architects, authors, and musicians. Irwin, a California writer, sketches her fellow Californiacs with affectionate malice. Irwin's sketches still sting a century later, because the superlatives she mocked have only grown.
3789-preface-to-major-barbara-first-aid-:
Bernard Shaw wrote this preface to defend Major Barbara against critics who blamed his ideas on foreign thinkers. He protests the habit of tracing every bold view to Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Ibsen, Strindberg, or Tolstoy, and insists that English life itself supplies his material. The essay then traces his own debts to native reformers, from Mill, Dickens, Ruskin, and Carlyle to Butler, Henry George, and Morris.

Shaw's target is poverty, not philosophy, and he points to Peter Shirley, a worker turned out to starve at forty because younger hands cost less. The preface argues that society must organize itself to end such everyday infamy. Readers who want Shaw in full fighting trim will find an essay as lively as the play, and a clear guide to its moral argument.
3795-under-the-lilacs:
Louisa May Alcott writes this children's tale around an old shut up house, an elm avenue, and lilacs nodding over a high wall. A mysterious dog leads two girls to the house's secrets, and soon Ben, a runaway boy with a circus past, finds a place among new friends. Miss Celia takes him in, Thorny, an invalid boy, studies plants with him, and Betty, Bows, and arrows, and speaking pieces fill the happy chapters.

Trouble comes with runaways, lost children, and a detective named Thornton, but kindness wins the day. Ben prefers ants and bugs to long plant names, and dodges his lessons with charm. Readers who know Little Women will find the same warmth here, with animals, gardens, and second chances at the heart of the story.
4292-copyright-basics:
The United States Copyright Office issued this short guide to the basics of copyright for ordinary readers. It explains what copyright covers, who owns it, how long it lasts, and what notice and registration mean. It also sets out the rights of owners and the limits that let others use works fairly.

Written in plain official prose, the booklet avoids legal advice and sticks to the statute's main points. It suits writers, teachers, and librarians who need a first orientation. For fuller rules, readers are pointed to the longer circulars, but this guide gives the groundwork in a small compass.
470-heretics:
G. K. Chesterton attacks the reigning ideas of his day in this 1905 essay volume. He takes on Shaw, Wells, Kipling, and other modern prophets, arguing that their heresies hide a loss of faith in life itself. Chesterton defends orthodoxy, wonder, and common sense with paradox, jest, and sudden thrusts.

Essays move from art and science to marriage, progress, and the press, each closing with a twist. His exuberant style makes foes feel like friends even as he beats them. The book endures as a lively defense of tradition, written by a journalist who loved argument and never feared a bold claim.
5626-the-motormaniacs:
Lloyd Osbourne wrote The Motormaniacs, a collection opening with its title story about motoring, romance, and social comedy. The narrator wanders off with an engaged girl, who notes that everybody else seems afraid of her. He claims sterner stuff and begs to know what she found to like in Gerard Malcolm. He also wants to know what Malcolm found in her, and what everyone said, until she answers that what he wants to know would fill a book.

Other stories include The Great Bubble Syndicate and Coal Oil Johnny Jones. Readers get light Edwardian tales of cars, money, and flirtation, written with Osbourne's easy humor.
5684-the-metaphysical-elements-of-ethics:
Immanuel Kant's Metaphysical Elements of Ethics, translated by Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, sets out the system of duties that follows from pure practical reason. Kant opens with a question. Does every practical philosophy need a metaphysic, a set of rational concepts free from sense experience? He answers yes, since duties must rest on such principles to bind all rational beings. The book then sorts duties toward oneself and toward others.

Its central demand is inward as well as outward: knowing a duty is not enough unless awareness of that duty itself moves the will to act. Readers meet a strict, spare ethics in which good conduct is measured by principle rather than by feeling or reward. The work pairs naturally with Kant's earlier foundations of morals, and it still shapes debates about duty, rights, and moral law.
5775-problems-of-conduct-an-introductory:
Problems of Conduct offers an introductory survey of ethics in two parts: the evolution of morality and the theory of morality. Early chapters ask when personal and social morality emerged, how conscience developed, and whether morality can rest on conscience alone. Later chapters take up the basis of right and wrong, the meaning of duty, the judgment of character, and the solution of personal and social problems.

You get a clear, question-driven textbook, written for students meeting ethics for the first time. Each chapter states its problem plainly, weighs answers, and leaves room for judgment. The book suits readers who want philosophy without jargon, and teachers seeking a structured path through duty, character, and the moral life.
6366-the-principles-of-aesthetics:
DeWitt H. Parker, professor of philosophy at the University of Michigan, grew this book from lectures to his students, seeking scientific accuracy with freedom of style and something of art's own inspiration. Though meant for students, he hopes it will appeal more widely. The chapters run from purpose and method and the definition of art through intrinsic value. The elements and structure of aesthetic experience follow, with the problem of evil solved through tragic, pathetic, and comic.

A standard of taste follows, then music, poetry, prose, painting, and sculpture, with beauty in industrial arts and architecture, and art's function in morality and religion. Parker argues that great personality wins pity and admiration through personal suffering and fortitude, not through abstract principle alone. The book is a clear, systematic aesthetics, built for readers who want reasons for what they feel before pictures and poems.
6752-study-and-stimulants-or-the-use-of-:
A. Arthur Reade edits a study of stimulants and narcotics in relation to intellectual life, drawn from personal letters by men of letters and of science. His introduction notes a fierce, long dispute: opposite views, each argued with skill, leave readers puzzled by blessings and bannings heaped on tobacco and alcohol. Doctors' authority alone cannot settle it.

The question at the heart is plain: do stimulants give more strength, clearer mind, and better work, or do they steal it? Writers and scientists answer in their own words. Study and Stimulants is a curious, historic survey of drink, drugs, and the working brain.
8072-national-epics:
Kate Milner Rabb published National Epics in 1896 as an introduction to the study of the great epic poems. Her preface explains the need: many readers of literary taste find the epics inaccessible, and busy lives leave little time to explore the realms of gold alone. She therefore condenses each epic, keeping characteristic epithets and what Matthew Arnold called the simple grandeur of the style, so that readers can grasp each poem's story and spirit.

The volume serves as a guidebook to the world's heroic poetry, from ancient epics to their national successors. It is meant to send readers on to the poems themselves, not to replace them. For students and general readers, it remains a friendly doorway into a form that can seem forbidding, and a reminder of how nations told their founding stories.
8197-india-s-love-lyrics:
Laurence Hope, the pen name of Adela Florence Cory Nicolson, wrote India's Love Lyrics from a life spent mostly in India. Born in 1865 and educated in England, she joined her father in India at sixteen, married Colonel Malcolm H. Nicolson in 1889, and died by suicide two months after his death in 1904. Her lyrics open with Less than the Dust, a poem of abasement before a lord: less than the dust beneath his chariot wheel, less than the rust that never stained his sword.

Hope's poems speak in the voice of Indian lovers, with passion, longing, and devotion, in a style that made her famous in Edwardian England. Modern readers may question her ventriloquism, but her music and feeling remain striking. The collection is a landmark of Anglo-Indian verse, and a poignant record of its author's own sorrows.
8565-a-book-of-german-lyrics:
Friedrich Bruns, then a German teacher at the University of Wisconsin, gathered this school anthology of German lyric poems with notes and a vocabulary. Goethe opens the book, followed by Schiller, Uhland, and other well-known German poets, with each poem printed in German. Short notes explain hard words and turns of phrase, so students can read the poems in the original language.

Famous pieces sit beside shorter songs about spring, parting, night, and home, including the Erlking, the Fisher, and the King's son of Thule. The notes and word lists keep the focus on reading and understanding, not on literary theory. For a learner, it offers a graded path into German poetry; for a general reader, it gives a compact shelf of the songs Germans themselves long sang and quoted.
8591-french-lyrics:
Arthur Graves Canfield, professor of Romance languages and literatures at the University of Michigan, selected and edited French Lyrics, with an introduction and notes. His preface states the book's aim: as an introduction to the reading and study of French lyric poetry, hoping to make that poetry more widely known and more justly appreciated.

Canfield's anthology gathers French lyric poems across centuries, with notes for students learning the language and the tradition. Readers get a textbook anthology, scholarly and readable, for classroom or self-study. The book suits students of French, and lovers of lyric poetry who want a guided introduction to France's song tradition.
874-a-history-of-aeronautics:
E. Charles Vivian wrote this one-volume history of aeronautics, noting that heavier-than-air flight was then less than two decades old, and dirigible flight only a little older. The mass of trials and triumphs forced him to select, and he chose the pioneers, machines, and flights that mattered most.

Vivian covers balloons, airships, and aeroplanes, with the men who built and flew them, and the science that slowly mastered the air. His prose is clear and popular, aimed at readers who want the story whole. The book is a solid early survey of flight, written while its heroes were still alive and its future open.
a-book-of-german-lyrics: Friedrich Bruns edits a collection of German lyrics with their poets in order. Goethe leads the volume, followed by Schiller, Uhland, and other lyric poets of the German tradition. The poems include songs of welcome and parting, May songs, lake songs, and ballads such as the Erlking. The selection gives English readers a broad survey of German lyric poetry in its classic forms.
a-history-of-aeronautics:
E. Charles Vivian surveys the whole story of flight in one large volume, from old legends to the planes and airships of 1920. His foreword admits the record is scattered and that he must choose what to include. Part one follows the aeroplane from early trials through the Wright brothers and the war years.

Later parts cover design from 1903 to 1920, balloons and dirigibles from their beginnings, Santos-Dumont, military airships, and the growth of aircraft engines type by type. Vivian names the key flights, such as the Channel crossing and the London to Manchester race. The book serves as a broad early record of how flying began.
a-lie-never-justifiable-a-study-in-ethic: Henry Clay Trumbull studies in ethics whether a lie is ever justifiable. His opening chapter asks the question of the ages and weighs two proffered answers. Army prison life, killing an enemy, and lying to him test the argument. Trumbull concludes, as his title says, that a lie is never justifiable.
amusements-in-mathematics: Henry Ernest Dudeney offers amusements in mathematics, from arithmetical and algebraical problems to geometrical puzzles. The book invites readers to play with numbers, shapes, and logic, solving each puzzle by wit rather than heavy learning. Dudeney, a master puzzler, made mathematics a pastime for the general reader. The puzzles reward patience and a fresh look, and many still charm solvers today.
ancient-and-modern-physics: Thomas Edgar Willson writes on ancient and modern physics, in chapters that move from old theories of nature to the physics of his own day. The book compares what the ancients believed about matter and motion with modern experiment. Willson's survey suits readers curious about how physical science grew out of philosophy.
applied-eugenics: Paul Popenoe and Roswell Hill Johnson set out a 1918 case for eugenics, moving from heredity and natural selection to marriage, birth rates, immigration, and war. Chapters weigh nature against nurture, survey mental traits, and then argue for limits on groups the authors call dysgenic. Later sections apply the same program to taxes, farm life, schools, wages, housing, and religion. The book is a period document of early genetic thought, and its claims about human worth now read as dated and contested.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aesthetics:
Aesthetics may be defined as training in right thinking and right feeling about art. A. G. Baumgarten made it part of philosophy. Its domain, in Wolff's system, is indistinct presentations and sensuous taste's canons, from aisthanesthai, to perceive and feel. Growth followed into a philosophy of nature and art's beautiful, and finally a science of the fine arts on philosophical principles.

Natural beauty, particular works, pure beauty, and philosophical questions get thorough treatment sometimes and mere touches other times. Applied aesthetics describes and values particular works accurately. Technical aesthetics trains the art student in single productions. Art history records art's development on a definite plan. Aesthetics must seek the deepest grounds of pleasure in art, in nature's laws and above all in the mind's laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apologetics:
Apologetics is presented here as the theological science that explains and defends the Christian religion. The word comes from Greek apologia, meaning defence. The article takes apology in its old sense: a spoken defence against a spoken attack, a rebuttal of false charge, or a justification of conduct wrongly blamed. Socrates' Apology and Newman's Apologia stand as models of that older use, far from the modern sense of saying sorry.

From that definition the long article builds its field, covering the grounds for belief, answers to objections, and the history of Christian defence from the early apologists onward. It treats apologetics as a reasoned science, not as mere assertion, and orders its arguments so that a reader can follow how faith answers doubt step by step. Students of theology will find a survey of method as well as matter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apotactics:
Apotactics, from a Greek word meaning to renounce, were followers of a heresy that arose in the third century and spread through western and southern Asia Minor. Almost all we know comes from Epiphanius. They called themselves renunciators because they scrupulously gave up all private property, and they also took the name Apostolics, claiming to follow the apostles' way of life. Epiphanius counts them a branch of the Tatianists, akin to Encratites and Cathari.

He charges them in sharp terms. Their sacraments and mysteries differ from the church's. They pride themselves on extreme poverty, stir division by foolish superstitions, and refuse reconciliation to those who have once fallen. They condemn marriage like their parent sect and reject Scripture, grounding their heresy in the apocryphal Acts of Andrew and Thomas. The entry preserves a hostile portrait of a sect known only through its enemies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archontics:
The Archontics, from archon, prince or ruler, were a Gnostic sect in Palestine and Armenia around the middle of the fourth century. Epiphanius, the earliest Christian writer to describe them, tells of a young Palestinian priest named Peter, convicted of Gnostic errors, deposed, and expelled by Bishop Aëtius. Peter fled to a part of Arabia that was a centre of Ebionite teaching, then in old age, apparently but not really converted, returned to Palestine.

There he lived as an anchorite, a solitary, in a cave near Jerusalem, drawing followers by austere life and extreme poverty. Shortly before Emperor Constantius died in 361, Eutactus came from Egypt, visited Peter, took in his doctrines, and carried them to Greater and Lesser Armenia. Epiphanius excommunicated Peter, and the sect soon died out. The entry preserves a sect known through one hostile witness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aztecs:
The Aztecs, probably named from Nahuatl words for heron and man, meaning people of the heron, were the Mexica tribe of aboriginal Mexico. The Mexica proper held islands at the center of Lake Tezcuco and a few shore settlements, numbering about thirty thousand souls in 1519. Their central settlement, Tenochtitlan, was founded about 1325. Before the lake settlement, their history is uncertain, resting on fragmentary picture writings.

Those documents trace constant wanderings from places such as Aztlan, Place of the Heron, and Chicomoztoc, Seven Caves, mostly set north of Mexico. The Mexica were the last Nahuatl speakers to reach the great lake shore, and their language links to Shoshonian tongues of the Northwest. The long article closes with a warning. Its sources, from sixteenth-century Indian records to Clavigero's history, demand critical caution, colored by their times and by personal bias. Nahuatl literature itself began soon after Mexico's press arrived in 1535.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-statis:
An entry on church statistics, the counting and tabulating of ecclesiastical life by the same methods as general statistics. Personal statistics observe people, material statistics observe things and actions, and theory refines practice until materials can be sifted and their links found. Church statistics need no separate technique, though their province has its own bounds, shading into economics and ethics.

The method gathers totals to investigate varied conditions, events, and omissions, handling data so that government, church, and national life can be known correctly. History shows city, state, and church tabulating from time immemorial, however roughly, from family and tribe records onward. The entry surveys the field, its divisions, and its growth, arguing that exactness matters as much for church figures as for civil ones, whether statistics count as an exact science or not.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-demoniacs:
A doctrinal entry on people said to be controlled by a demon, with its centre in the New Testament. Ancient peoples nearly everywhere held that evil spirits could seize a person, and the Gospels give such cases special weight. Casting out demons stands out among the miracles of Christ, and the entry treats those accounts as the measure for judging other claims.

Mark opens in the Capharnaum synagogue with a man bearing an unclean spirit. Peter sums up the mission of Jesus as healing those weighed down by the devil. Miracles here count as both deeds and words, signs of power over evil. Later pages weigh the evidence for real possession and commend a study of the cases, even for readers who doubt its wider claims.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ethics:
Many writers regard ethics as any scientific treatment of the moral order, divided into theological and philosophical ethics. What is usually meant by ethics is philosophical ethics, or moral philosophy, treated here. Moral philosophy is a division of practical philosophy. Theoretical philosophy deals with being, the order of things not dependent on reason, seeking knowledge of it in its ultimate causes. Practical philosophy concerns what ought to be: the order of human acts depending on reason.

Practical philosophy is divided into logic and ethics. Logic orders the intellect and teaches the method of acquiring truth, while ethics directs the will; the former's object is the true, the latter's the good. Hence ethics is the science of the moral rectitude of human acts according to natural reason's first principles. Logic and ethics are normative sciences, prescribing norms for human activities and showing how a man ought to act.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugenics:
Eugenics, a word meaning good breeding, is the subject of this long reference article on a movement then new. It defines the field as the study of forces under social control that may improve or harm the traits of future generations. Sir Francis Galton fixed both the word and the definition. The article follows his work from breeding racehorses to his law of heredity, his studies of able families, and the challenge from Mendel's laws.

Much of the piece sets Catholic teaching beside modern eugenics. It divides the movement into positive eugenics, which favors parenthood among the fit, and negative eugenics, which discourages it among the unfit. It weighs race poisons such as drink, disease, and lead. The Church, it argues, backs sound breeding done on right lines, but puts moral life and eternal life ahead of civic worth, and guards marriage with rules on consent, kinship, and banns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermeneutics:
Hermeneutics is the science of interpreting the Bible rightly, the set of rules that guides sound exegesis, or explanation, of Sacred Scripture. The name comes from a Greek word linked to Hermes, the reputed messenger and interpreter of the gods, but usage has narrowed it to biblical interpretation alone. Just as grammar guides speech and logic guides reasoning, hermeneutics guides readers who want to explain the Bible correctly.

Early Christians explained Scripture without a formal science of the subject, yet correct readings always match its canons. The entry sets out why such rules are needed, how the science grew slowly from practice to theory, and how Catholic and non-Catholic writers across the ages handled hard passages. It also treats special problems, such as reading Scripture in light of history and natural science.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-history-of-ph:
This long article surveys physics from ancient times to the nineteenth century under nearly thirty heads. It begins with ancient physics and early Christian scholars, then moves through Arabian physics and Latin scholasticism. It pauses over the Paris school's doctrines of impetus, the vacuum debates of 1277, and the earth's motion and plurality of worlds.

Later sections follow the Copernican revolution, Galileo's work, Descartes, and Newton's synthesis. They continue with experimental physics, the undulatory theory of light, the theory of electricity and magnetism, and theories of heat. Figures such as Jordanus, Oresme, Purbach, Regiomontanus, Cusa, Kepler, and Gilbert each get their place. Readers gain a full map of how physical thought changed across two thousand years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-homiletics:
Homiletics is the science of composing and delivering a sermon or other religious discourse. It covers the sermon, the homily, and catechetical instruction, and since the nineteenth century it has counted, in Germany above all, among pastoral theology's branches. The Standard Dictionary calls it rhetoric's branch for sermons and homilies, but many hold homiletics distinct from rhetoric.

Christ preached himself and sent his apostles to do the same. His preaching took two forms: missionary preaching to unbelievers and ministerial preaching to those already in the faith, exemplified by the discourse after the Last Supper. The entry traces preaching from its homily roots through its history, and returns at the end to whether homiletics stands apart from rhetoric.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kalocsa-bacs:
Kalocsa-Bacs was a Hungarian archdiocese embracing sees founded by St. Stephen in 1010. How Kalocsa and Bacs were founded, and how they related, stayed uncertain for long. Fejér thought Stephen founded both as independent sees, with Ladislaus later uniting Bacs to Kalocsa. Katona held instead that Bacs arose by dividing Kalocsa, with reunion in 1135. Városy solved the question: Bacs never existed as an independent see at all.

Kalocsa's archbishops had simply moved their residence to Bacs at times, until an independent chapter grew up there. In 1135 the union was confirmed, and the archdiocese took the name Kalocsa-Bacs. Bacs stayed the archbishops' residence and burial place until Mohács in 1526, when it fell to the Turks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-metaphysics:
Metaphysics is that part of philosophy which treats the most general and basic principles beneath all reality and all knowledge. The entry covers its name, definition, rejection, relations to other sciences and to theology, method, history, and doctrine of being. Its name comes from Greek meta ta phusika, a title Andronicus of Rhodes gave about A.D. 70 to Aristotle's treatises that follow the Physics.

Aristotle himself called this field the theological science, since it crowns itself in God's nature, and first philosophy, since it treats first causes and ranks first in worth. His editor, missing both titles, named the collection after the physics. Later commentators then sought deeper reasons for the name, reading it as the science of being as being, of immaterial being, of the most abstract and universal notions, and of first principles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-micmacs:
The Micmacs, called Souriquois by the early French, were the easternmost Algonquin tribe and probably the first visited by a white man. They once held Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Cape Breton, with parts of New Brunswick, Quebec, and southwestern Newfoundland. In the original division of land among the eastern Algonquins, they held third rank, after the Ottawa and the Abenaki, their province being known as Migmagig.

They welcomed the French and their faith, preached by secular priests, Jesuits, Recollects, and Capuchins. Father Biard, writing in 1611, described them as mild and peaceful and reckoned them at three to three and a half thousand. The Capuchins opened the first high school in New France for them and the settlers, and a 1633 report to Rome placed a Micmac mission at Port Royal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mosaics:
Mosaics are pictures and patterns built from small pieces of marble, glass, ceramic or precious stone. The pieces are set in cement to form an ornamental whole. The word's lineage runs from Greek mouseion, appertaining to the Muses, through Latin opus musivum into French mosaique. Strictly the term fits work in small cubes, opus tessellatum or vermiculatum, but usage has widened.

It now covers opus sectile, pieces ground exactly to a geometric or foliated design, and the pavement work of Roman houses. It also covers the great wall mosaics of early Christian and Byzantine churches. The entry follows the craft from Greek and Roman floors through Ravenna, Rome and Constantinople to medieval Italy. It describes materials, setting methods, gold grounds and the workshops that kept the art alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-munkacs:
Munkacs is a Greek Catholic diocese in Hungary, suffragan to Gran, dating from the fifteenth century. Greek Ruthenians who had emigrated to Hungary a generation before 1254 first answered to Przemysl. In 1458 a document of King Mathias first mentions Munkacs as a parish with episcopal jurisdiction. It was probably founded between 1439 and 1458.

Its history intertwines with the Basilian monastery at Csernekhegy near Munkacs, supposedly founded in 1360 by Duke Theodore Koriatovics but demonstrably as late as 1418. The entry divides its story into three periods. Expansion efforts lasted until union with Rome in 1641, then came the years to canonical erection in 1771, and its modern course, with bishops, parishes and the Ruthenian faithful it serves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-numismatics:
Numismatics, the science of coins and medals, reads money as evidence of the cultures that struck it. Every piece reflects the economic, political, and artistic conditions of its age, so the field splits by civilization and joins archaeology, history, and Oriental studies.

The entry separates descriptive numismatography from numismatology, which weighs coins as art and economics. It traces the science from collectors' cabinets to Eckhel's scientific treatment of ancient coins in 1790 and nineteenth-century work on modern issues. Aquinas on money opens the historical survey. Aquinas treated money and coinage in his De Regimine Principis, a point the entry recalls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-old-catholics:
The Old Catholics organized in German lands to reject the dogma of papal infallibility defined in 1870. Nearly 1,400 Germans declared that September that infallibility contradicted the church's traditional faith, cheered by liberal scholars, politicians, and press across Europe.

Munich's archbishop excommunicated Döllinger in April 1871, yet a congress at Munich that September drew over 300 delegates from German, Austrian, and Swiss lands. The entry follows their bishops, congresses, and churches in Germany, Austria, Switzerland, and the Netherlands. The first Old Catholic Congress met at Munich on 22 to 24 September 1871. More than 300 delegates from German, Austrian, and Swiss lands attended that congress.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-diploma:
Papal diplomatics is the science of ancient official documents, above all those from the chanceries of popes, kings, emperors, and other recognised authorities. The word should mean the science of diplomas, and a diploma once meant only a travel permit on the public posting service, or a veteran's discharge with privileges. Renaissance scholars wrongly took diploma for any charter, and the wider sense stuck.

Medieval forgery forced watchfulness over papal bulls and royal charters, and the Holy See's chancery set a strong example. Gregory VII even withheld his lead seal from a bull, fearing foes might misuse it. Mabillon's De Re Diplomatica gave the science its classic form, and later pages lay out the marks of genuine bulls, seals, scripts, and formulas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poor-catholic:
The Poor Catholics were a mendicant order organised in 1208 to win the Waldenses back to the Church and fight the heresies of the day, above all the Albigensians. Their recruits came from the Poor Men of Lyons, the Waldenses' original name, but Innocent III renamed them Poor Catholics to set them apart from the heretics they had left.

The Albigensians taught a dualism of two eternal principles. One, evil, authored the material world. The other, good, authored the spiritual world. They rejected marriage and animal food and preached renunciation of matter. The Waldenses, by contrast, were a popular movement born of neglect by clergy who minded temporal affairs over souls. The entry sets both movements against a church where public preaching had grown rare and the people hungered for the bread of life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-relics:
Relics takes its name from the Latin reliquiae, matching the Greek leipsana, a word used before Christianity in its modern sense. It means an object, above all part of a body or clothing, kept as a memorial of a departed saint. Such veneration is partly a primitive instinct, and belongs to other faiths too. At Athens the supposed remains of Oedipus and Theseus won honours close to worship. Plutarch's accounts of moving the bodies of Demetrius and Phocion foreshadow medieval practice.

The Christian cult grows from early examples. Hair of Saint James and oil multiplied by Bishop Narcissus were venerated when Eusebius wrote about 325. Augustine's City of God tells of miracles from Holy Land soil. The idea widened to objects that had touched a saint. The Church ordered their keeping and honour, and relics stay a greater double feast wherever they are preserved.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rubrics:
Rubric comes from rubrica, the red earth carpenters used to mark wood for cutting. Soon red passed from titles to remarks on a text. Liturgical collections adopted the custom to distinguish instructions from prayer formulas, so rubric became the term for rules of Divine service and sacraments. Gavanti dated its liturgical sense to the Venice Breviary of 1550, but it appears in fourteenth-century manuscripts.

The word marks general laws or a particular indication, always explaining the text's use — hence the old saying about reading the red to grasp the black. In liturgical books red characters show what should be done and black what should be recited. Rubrics may be defined as rules for reciting the Divine Office, celebrating Mass, and administering the sacraments. They resemble ceremonies but differ: ceremonies are external attitudes and movements, while rubrics bear on the essential rite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-synoptics:
The Synoptics are the first three canonical Gospels, Matthew, Mark, and Luke, named since Griesbach's time about 1790. Unlike John, they can be set side by side section by section, so the eye catches at once what they share and what belongs to only two or one of them. A harmony in parallel columns makes the likeness plain.

Brief as the three sketches are, they run parallel in 330 to 370 verses, about a third of their whole account, and nearly all of Mark reappears in Matthew and Luke. They agree in choosing the same healings and discourses from a far larger stock, and in ordering Christ's life from John's preaching through Galilee. The entry then weighs explanations for the likeness, closing with studies to 1911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-will-and-test:
This entry sets out the church law on what clergy could leave by will, from Roman law through the early councils. Roman law let clerics pass on property by will, but bishops could not bequeath goods gained during their episcopate; those went to pious uses in their diocese. Goods held before becoming bishop, and the property of clerics who died without a will, passed to lawful heirs or, failing heirs, to their churches.

Early canons barred lower clergy as well as bishops from willing away church-gained wealth, and ordered lists of private versus church goods so they could not be mixed. Private wealth from family or other outside sources later won recognition. Bishops faced anathema for naming pagan or heretical heirs, and councils at Agde, Seville, Rheims, and Paris fenced the rules further. The councils guarded church property against heirs who grabbed it after an intestate bishop died.
copyright-basics:
Copyright Basics is a plain-language guide issued by the Copyright Office of the Library of Congress. Written for authors, artists, publishers, and users of creative work, it explains the federal system that protects original writing, music, and pictures. The guide answers basic questions in short sections and plain terms. It sets out what copyright means, who may claim it, and how long protection lasts.

Sections move through which works qualify for protection and which ideas stay free for anyone to use. Readers learn why publication matters, what a copyright notice should look like, and where it should appear. Later pages cover registration forms, required deposits, transfers of ownership, and the ending of old transfers. A closing section explains protection in other countries, giving newcomers a clear first map of American copyright rules.
doe-osti-17019148-direct-ink-write-metho: 3D-printing ceramics got its DOE methods report, and this text covers direct ink write techniques. The pages detail the pastes and the prints. The kilns get their inkjet. The methods were written. The prints were ceramic. The kilns got inkjet.
doe-osti-2588973-rag-for-flag-ai-assista: FLAG the physics code got its AI assistant, and this DOE report covers RAG for the codebase. The pages detail the AI help. The code users get their copilot. The code was FLAG. The assistance was AI. The users got copilots.
doe-osti-2997653-next-generation-perovsk: Perovskite solar got its next generation, and this DOE report improves, stabilizes, and lead-seals the cells. The pages detail the record-setting work. The solar folks get their roadmap. The cells were perovskite. The work was record-setting. The folks were solar.
doe-osti-2999883-arms-control-developmen: The rulebook for future arms deals got its DOE draft, and this text lays out the yardsticks. The pages detail the criteria. The policymakers get their framework. The draft was ACDCs. The criteria were detailed. The framework was policymaker. The yardsticks were DOE's.
doe-osti-3005570-beam-tuning-setups-for-: Drift tube linacs got beam-tuned, and this DOE text covers the setup methods. The pages detail the findings. The accelerator folks get their guide. The linacs were drift tube. The guide was accelerator. The methods were setup. The linacs were tube.
doe-osti-3028268-high-energy-neutrino-ph: Neutrinos got high-energy-physicked, and this DOE text covers the physics. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their data. The physics was high energy. The data were physicist. The energy were high. The physics were neutrino. The data were DOE.
doe-osti-3097336-persistent-dynamics: DOE researcher Dharmesh Patel reports on Persistent DynAMICS, a project whose name promises staying power in a fast-changing technical field. The report documents the project's aims and technical approach. Details are thin in the catalog record, but the title signals work meant to keep a dynamic system running reliably over time.
doe-osti-3374042-dynamic-multipoles-in-t: RCS got multipole-dynamicked, and this DOE text covers dynamic multipoles. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their data. The multipoles were dynamic. The data were physicist. The RCS were findings. The dynamic were multipoles. The physicists were data.
heretics:
G K Chesterton published Heretics in 1905, a set of essays arguing with the famous men and moods of his day. Chapters take up Rudyard Kipling, Bernard Shaw, H G Wells, George Moore, and the yellow press, along with Christmas, Omar Khayyam, and the institution of the family. His opening chapter insists that orthodoxy, having a definite creed, matters more than clever doubt.

Chesterton attacks the negative spirit that only tears down, using paradox, jokes, and sudden common sense. The book made his reputation as a debater readers could enjoy even while disagreeing. It also sets up his later Orthodoxy, since many heretics here are answered by the creed he defends there.
hieroglyphics: Machen argued for ecstasy in literature in this essay. The sacred art of writing, defended. The occult critic's manifesto. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. The book preserves that criticism. Scholars will consult it.
laughable-lyrics:
Edward Lear called Laughable Lyrics his fourth book of nonsense. It mixes poems, songs, botany, and music in one playful volume. A Gutenberg note points readers to an illustrated version with music files.

Lear invents creatures, plants, and places that obey no real rules. His rhymes bounce along with cheerful absurdity from page to page. Drawings by the author add to the fun throughout. Children and adults have loved his nonsense for generations. This late collection shows his gift undimmed, still turning language into a game. His invented words often sound like real English gone cheerfully wrong. Singable rhymes make many pieces work aloud for family reading.
laurier-a-study-in-canadian-politics:
John Wesley Dafoe published Laurier: A Study in Canadian Politics at Toronto in 1922. He dedicated it to E. H. Macklin, a constant friend. Three parts treat Laurier's rise, empire ties, and fifteen years as premier.

Dafoe notes that Skelton's life of Laurier is the official biography. His own study offers a sharper political reading instead. Sir Wilfrid Laurier led Canada through a long, changing era. Dafoe weighs his climb to power and his handling of empire questions. The book suits readers of Canadian political history. Dafoe later shaped Canadian journalism as a major editor. His political eye here is trained, partisan, and clear.
modern-spanish-lyrics:
Elijah Clarence Hills and S. Griswold Morley edited this textbook of Spanish lyric poetry for Henry Holt in 1913. Hills taught Romance languages at Colorado College; Morley was at the University of Colorado. The book carries an introduction, notes, and a vocabulary for students. A section on Spanish versification opens the contents.

The poems begin with España and a set of old romances, or ballads. Abenámar, Fonte-frida, and the Count Arnaldos represent that tradition. Gil Vicente and Saint Teresa of Jesus follow with songs and devotional verse. Despite the title's modern, the anthology reaches back centuries, giving American students a short history of Spanish song in one volume.
moral-science-a-compendium-of-ethics:
Alexander Bain, professor of logic at the University of Aberdeen, published this compendium of ethics in 1869. It companions his Mental Science, a compendium of psychology. Part One lays out the theory of ethics. Bain begins with the ethical standard, the moral faculty, and the freedom of the will.

His summary states the standard plainly: the welfare of society, realized through enforced rules of conduct. Obligatory morality is imposed under penalty, as law proper. Later sections classify duties and the moral code, and relate ethics to politics and theology. Bain writes as a utilitarian philosopher, building morality on happiness and habit rather than revelation.
nasa-tm-19650017036-longitudinal-aerodyn:
William B Igoe, Richard J Re, and Francis J Capone at Langley reported tunnel results in June 1962 for an unusual aircraft model. The model, at one-thirtieth scale, had a canard layout, with a small wing ahead of the main wing. Its main wing had an aspect ratio of three and six tenths. Speeds ran from well below sound to near it.

The catalog note links the shape to a nuclear powered aircraft study. The team measured lengthwise, or longitudinal, behavior across that speed range. A canard layout promises control benefits but needs careful proof. Their data show how this model behaved as speed rose toward the speed of sound.
nasa-tm-19650019829-research-and-develop:
Only body pages survive in the hosted sample for this essay on research and development economics, with no readable title page or author line. The pages argue that advances in technology are reshaping political life as well as industry. One example given is the fierce Senate debate over the Communications Satellite Corporation, where debate was cut off for the first time in decades.

The writer urges readers to understand the forces behind such change. Economic measures shift along with the technology itself. The closing thought is firm: the future world will be different. As a period piece, it captures official thinking about research spending and national growth.
nasa-tm-19660020176-longitudinal-aerodyn:
Arvo A Luoma at Langley measured lengthwise behavior at transonic speeds for a V/STOL airplane shape, in a December 1961 memorandum later declassified. The shape joins a fixed delta wing with outer panels that can change sweep. Panels of that kind promise better slow flight without giving up the delta's fast flight. V/STOL aircraft were meant to rise vertically, then fly like normal airplanes.

Transonic speed is where such mixed designs face their hardest test. Luoma reports the longitudinal aerodynamic characteristics measured for the layout. The data let designers judge whether movable outer panels earned their weight and complexity. Many vertical flight concepts of the era lived or died on tunnel results like these.
nasa-tm-19670030539-mars-thermophysics:
W. P. McNutt, Barbara Maye, and Nancy McHugh compiled this bibliography at the Redstone Scientific Information Center in Alabama in September 1967. Numbered RSIC-657, its subject is Mars thermophysics, the heat behavior of the planet Mars. It was prepared for the Thermophysics Division of the Space Sciences Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center.

About five hundred annotated citations cover Mars literature from the late nineteenth century through early 1967. Only thermophysics was admitted: results of experiments and analyses in the parts of the electromagnetic spectrum that reveal a planet's thermal state. References on possible life on Mars and on space vehicle design were deliberately excluded. Sources searched ranged from astronomy yearbooks and defense holdings to NASA abstract tapes and Jet Propulsion Laboratory summaries. Careful screening removed duplicates, and entries were arranged alphabetically by author under eight subject groupings.
nasa-tm-19670030653-history-of-aeronauti:
Katherine Murphy Dickson, of the Library of Congress in Washington, D.C., compiled this preliminary bibliography on the history of aeronautics and astronautics. The work was sponsored by the NASA Historical Staff, in the Office of Policy Analysis. A foreword from the NASA Historian, dated May 1967, introduces the volume.

The foreword traces practical human flight from the lower atmosphere at the century's start to orbital spaceflight less than sixty years later. A Moon landing then stood close ahead. Space technology's history, it observes, had not yet been well examined by historians, although technical writing and early analysis abounded. Dickson's listing, in large part a list of such lists, was meant as a working tool for historical record keeping and analysis. Being a first pass, it openly invites readers' ideas and comments to improve later editions.
nasa-tm-19690020329-preliminary-performa:
James C. Wood and five Lewis Research Center co-authors report a gas-bearing turboalternator's early performance in this report. The Brayton cycle machine uses gas-lubricated bearings and runs on argon. It operated through steady and transient modes for well over a thousand hours total.

During testing the machine started and stopped twenty-four times. Output at turbine design conditions reached the level the authors report, with a much higher maximum output also obtained. Temperatures never exceeded predicted values at design conditions. Bearings stayed within design clearance limits in all tests. The largest clearance changes came at the thrust bearings during full-load electrical transients. Gas bearings avoid oil, a key gain for closed power systems.
nasa-tm-19710005468-low-subsonic-aerodyn:
George M. Ware and Bernard Spencer Jr. of the Langley Research Center wrote this report in January 1971. It measures the low-speed aerodynamics of a shuttle orbiter design. The model's delta wing could change its dihedral, the upward angle of the wings.

Tests ran in Langley's low-turbulence pressure tunnel. Slow flight is where an orbiter must land, so its manners there matter greatly. The team recorded lift, drag, and stability for the shape across the test range. A wing that folds to a new angle in flight might serve two flight regimes well. Studies like this one weighed that promise against real measured behavior.
nasa-tm-19710007778-longitudinal-aerodyn:
Theodore J. Goldberg and James C. Emery of the Langley Research Center wrote this report in February 1971. It gives the lengthwise aerodynamic traits of the Viking lander capsule at Mach 6. The capsule would carry Viking landers through the thin air of Mars, entering at hypersonic speed.

A small-scale model of the capsule was tested in a wind tunnel at that speed. Changing the flow's Reynolds number, the results show, had no effect on the aerodynamic coefficients. The afterbody likewise made no difference across the tested angles of attack. One prediction method matched the measurements reasonably well, while modified Newtonian theory overshot the normal-force and pitching-moment values.
nasa-tm-19710026939-longitudinal-aerodyn:
Charles D. Trescot Jr. of the Langley Research Center wrote this October 1971 memorandum, NASA TM X-2367, on a supersonic missile model's lengthwise behavior. The model had cruciform delta wings, set crosswise around the body. Three different small front wings, called canards, plus a trailing-edge flap on the horizontal wings, served as its controls.

Tests in the Langley Unitary Plan wind tunnel covered speeds from Mach 1.50 to Mach 4.63 across a wide range of attack angles. Trescot presents the static stability and control results as aerodynamic parameters plotted against Mach number. He notes that no detailed analysis of the results was attempted. Even so, the summary offers the data as a systematic source for checking analytical prediction methods against experiment.
national-epics:
Kate Milner Rabb published National Epics in 1896 as a first guide to the great long poems of many lands. Her preface says many readers with a taste for books could not reach the epics themselves. Busy lives left them no time to read the full poems.

Rabb retells each story in short form and keeps the poems' own stock phrases where she can. A brief sketch before each tale gives its length, verse form, and history. A chosen passage then shows one whole event in the poet's own words. She also traces how epics grew from songs sung for dead heroes.
podcast-joerogan-qd2eqKpqHcs:
