Jordan Peterson speculates on psychedelics and the birth of religion in this clip from the Joe Rogan Experience. Peterson asks whether ancient drug experiences shaped the stories and visions at the root of faith. It is one of his boldest theories, and Rogan is the perfect host for it.

Peterson points to cave art, rituals, and scripture that he thinks may record altered states. He argues the mushroom and other plants could have sparked ideas of gods and spirits. Rogan adds his own long history with psychedelic talk on the show. The segment is short, strange, and pure Peterson.
preface-to-major-barbara-first-aid-to-cr:
Bernard Shaw wrote this preface to his play Major Barbara under the subtitle First Aid to Critics, and began with a note of credit. The Euripidean verses in the second act are Professor Gilbert Murray's, from his Bacchae translation, to which the play stands indebted in more ways than one. Then Shaw turns on his reviewers. Whenever his view strays beyond an ordinary suburban churchwarden's, they derive him from Schopenhauer, Nietzsche, Ibsen, Strindberg, or Tolstoy, any heresiarch except a British one.

He pleads guilty to flattery at the compliment to his languages, then prosecutes his real case: Charles Lever's forgotten novel A Day's Ride. Which Dickens serialized and the public rejected, taught the child Shaw the tragicomic conflict between romantic imagination and real life, the very thing critics call Ibsenite in him. The preface is Shaw's criticism of his critics, and a short autobiography of an Irish imagination.
problems-of-conduct-an-introductory-surv:
Durant Drake, a teacher of ethics at Wesleyan University, turned his lectures into a plain survey of right and wrong printed at Boston in 1914. The course had first been given at the University of Illinois and was written for students and general readers alike.

Each chapter states a problem of conduct, weighs the main views, and ends with a list of readings for further study. Drake aims to make readers think for themselves rather than memorize rules. College classes get a clear first map of ethics, and private readers get guidance without hard terms.
progressive-morality-an-essay-in-ethics:
Thomas Fowler, president of Corpus Christi College and a professor of logic at Oxford, set out a scientific view of morals in an essay of 1884. He wrote for general readers, keeping the pages short, plain, and free of quarrels with other authors.

Fowler argues that ideas of right grow and change with knowledge, and that his views match those gaining ground among thoughtful people of his day. The essay grew apart from a larger work on morals left unfinished at a colleague's death. Readers get a calm Victorian statement of ethics as a growing science.
riley-love-lyrics:
James Whitcomb Riley's love lyrics are printed with life pictures by William B. Dyer, by Grosset and Dunlap of New York. Copyrights listed run from 1883 to 1905, across Riley's long career as a poet of the heart. He inscribes the book to the Elect of Love, whether side by side in rapture or sundered wide by seas.

A minstrel poem follows the inscription. Riley wishes he were a singer deft at weaving rondels such as rapture sings. He would loop his lyre across his breast and not rest until his knee found midnight banks of bud and flower beneath his lady's lattice bower. The set gathers his love poems in one dress.
russian-lyrics: Martha Gilbert Dickinson Bianchi put Russian lyrics into English verse in Russian Lyrics, Songs of Cossack, Lover, Patriot and Peasant. The book was issued in New York in 1916 under a copyright of 1910. A list of her other books heads the volume, among them The Kiss of Apollo, The Sin of Angels, A Cossack Lover, and A Modern Prometheus.
sappho-one-hundred-lyrics: Bliss Carman wrote Sappho, One Hundred Lyrics, dated 1907, under two mottoes. One calls Sappho a poet who broke off a fragment of her soul for later readers to guess at. The other, from E. B. Browning, hails Sappho with a halo of ebon hair on calmed brows and says none forgoes the leap who attains the repose.
searchlights-on-health-the-science-of-eu:
Prof. B. G. Jefferis and J. L. Nichols issued this health guide from Naperville, Illinois, in 1920. Nichols and Company sold it through agents across the country. The title page calls the book a guide to purity and strong manhood, with advice for girls, wives, and mothers.

Short extracts from doctors, clergy, and other named writers fill out the guidance. Pages cover love, courtship, and marriage, plus the care of the body and the home. The book shows what passed for sound counsel on sex and family life in its day, stated in plain moral terms for a wide public.
spirits-in-bondage-a-cycle-of-lyrics:
Clive Hamilton wrote Spirits in Bondage, a cycle of lyrics. Hamilton was the pen name of C. S. Lewis. Three parts shape the set. The Prison House comes first. Hesitation and The Escape follow. A note on the book's past calls it Lewis's first book. Heinemann released it in 1919. Most poems date from 1915 to 1918. Lewis then studied under W. T. Kirkpatrick. He trained at Oxford and served in the trenches.

The poems swing between two poles, the note says. One pole praises nature's beauty and plainness. The other states sharp claims about evil in the world. Lewis wrote to Arthur Greeves in September 1918. The book hangs on one idea, he said there. Nature is wholly devilish and ill-willed. God, if he exists, stands outside the world's frame. A motto line heads the set. It names a land and a love the singer shall never see.
stephen-a-douglas-a-study-in-american-po: Allen Johnson, who held the chair of history in Bowdoin College and once held it in Iowa College, wrote Stephen A. Douglas: A Study in American Politics. Macmillan printed the New York book in February 1908, under a copyright of that year. Johnson gives the book to Professor Jesse Macy, whose wisdom and kind ways, he says, have stirred a whole wave of students. A note at the front keeps first spellings as found, with the older form Douglass among them.
studies-in-civics:
James T. McCleary, once a teacher of civics and history at the State Normal School at Mankato, Minnesota, wrote Studies in Civics as a school textbook, revised to 1897. A picture of the United States Capitol fronts the book, and McCleary dedicates it to his own classes, whose questions shaped its contents.

His preface promises useful material in usable form. The Constitution gets a careful study of its full text rather than a bare abstract, yet every other branch of government gets its share too. The order begins with the town, where students can watch government at work, and rises step by step to government in general, with tables and documents packed into an appendix.
study-and-stimulants-or-the-use-of-intox:
Study and Stimulants, edited by A. Arthur Reade, asks what intoxicants and narcotics really do to the brain, drawing its evidence from personal communications by men of letters and of science. The full title promises the use of intoxicants and narcotics in relation to intellectual life.

Reade's introduction says the subject had seen fierce and long debate, with able men arguing opposite sides and doctors blessing and banning tobacco and alcohol alike. Do stimulants give strength, clearness, and staying power, or do they cloud the mind and weaken long effort? The book puts the questions to working writers and scientists and prints what they reported of their own habits and results.
taboo-and-genetics:
Taboo and Genetics, printed at London and New York in 1921, is a study of the biological, sociological, and psychological foundations of the family. Its three authors, M. M. Knight, Iva Lowther Peters, and Phyllis Blanchard, all doctors of philosophy, dedicate the book to their friend and teacher Frank Hamilton Hankins.

Part I, by Knight, treats the new biology and the sex problem in society. Its first chapter defines the problem: what sex is, how sexual reproduction arose, the advantage of sex in the chance of survival, and the difference between germ cells and body cells. Knight also marks the limits of biology in social questions, a caution the book keeps while weighing taboos on marriage and kinship.
the-agrarian-crusade-a-chronicle-of-the-:
Solon J. Buck wrote The Agrarian Crusade, a chronicle of the farmer in politics, printed at New Haven by Yale University Press in 1920 as volume 45 of the Chronicles of America set. This textbook printing carries a preface on the age's strains.

Buck calls swift growth with painful adjustment a lead trait of the last half century of United States history. In the West the change came so fast it near remade the land, and the frontier's passing took old freedom with it. Farm towns woke as complex trade regions where farmers had lost their first rank. Protest rose from that loss. Readers trace granges, alliances, and Populists as farmers fought railroads, banks, and trusts at the polls.
the-californiacs:
Inez Haynes Irwin opens The Californiacs with a rolling hymn to California. It produces, she says, the maximum of scenery and the minimum of weather. Its men, trees, vegetables, and even its fleas are the biggest anywhere. Its women, babies, flowers, and fruits are the most beautiful. California is the home of the movie, the Spanish mission, the golden poppy, and most American slang.

That California, Irwin repeats, is populated mainly with Californiacs. They are not confined to California: New York holds so large a colony of them that most New Yorkers can spot the symptoms at sight. The Californiac can talk of nothing but California, save to knock every other place on earth. He pities anyone born outside it, and though he often lives elsewhere, he never admits it is from choice.
the-children-s-hour-volume-3-of-10-stori: Eva March Tappan selected and arranged this third volume of The Children's Hour, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1907, gathering stories from the classics. Only the front matter is present here, including the editor's note thanking authors and publishers for leave to reprint. The note names Nathaniel Hawthorne's Wonder-Book and Tanglewood Tales among the sources.What the book holds past its front matter stays untold here.
the-golden-treasury-of-american-songs-an:
Frederic Lawrence Knowles edited The Golden Treasury of American Songs and Lyrics. L. C. Page and Company printed this new revised edition in Boston in 1899. His preface faults other sets of American verse. They share one flaw, he says: they include too much. They judge too little, in a bid for wide sales.

Knowles says no poem got in just because it was widely known. His aim is to keep about one hundred and fifty lyrics. They are to be the best lyrics of America. They are to be kept in a fit and lasting form. He owns that such an honor-roll is one man's judgment at best. The choice is a risk. The book is a strict, personal pick of American song. It is made to last rather than to please all tastes.
the-grammar-school-boys-in-summer-athlet:
H. Irving Hancock wrote The Grammar School Boys in Summer Athletics. Its subtitle is Or, Dick and Co. Make Their Fame Secure. A contents list has twenty-four chapters. They promise ball games, a swimming match, and school rivalries. The heads name North Grammars Play Real Ball and Ted Teall Faces the Storm. They name Hi's Swimming Challenge. Chapter I, A Jolt on a Quiet Day, opens out of doors.

Dave Darrin sighs that there is just one thing he keeps thinking about on such a day. Tom Reade guesses at once: supper. Darrin turns on him with a flash of disgust. Tom waits for the real answer. The easy teasing among Dick and his friends sets the tone. It is a boys' series tale. Summer sport, team pride, and small feuds carry the action.
the-mark-of-the-beast-and-other-horror-t: Rudyard Kipling's tales are gathered here under the title The Mark of the Beast. The record is labeled a Dover Horror Classics volume. Yet the pages call the book Mark of the Beast and Other Fantastical Tales, Fantasy Masterworks volume fifty. The two labels do not agree. Only a contents list is present, so the tales do not appear. It promises an introduction by Neil Gaiman and stories including The Phantom 'Rickshaw and The Strange Ride of Morrowbie Jukes. The Bisara of Pooree and My Own True Ghost Story follow.
the-metaphysical-elements-of-ethics:
Immanuel Kant's The Metaphysical Elements of Ethics, dated 1780 and translated by Thomas Kingsmill Abbott, opens with a preface on method. Kant argues that any subject with a philosophy needs a system of pure rational concepts independent of intuition: a metaphysic. Practical philosophy, the doctrine of duties, is no exception. Ethics must be presentable as a true science, systematically, not as an aggregate of separate doctrines.

Kant concedes that pure jurisprudence plainly needs such treatment, since it concerns only the formal side of free choice under laws. Ethics poses the harder question of whether duty can be purified of everything empirical, including feeling, and still move the will. A footnote defines the practical philosopher as one who makes the rational end the principle of his actions. For ethical duty, Kant says, the chief point is inner: consciousness of duty must itself become the spring of action.
the-motormaniacs:
Lloyd Osbourne's collection The Motormaniacs gathers four stories, named in its contents: the title story, The Great Bubble Syndicate, Coal Oil Johnny, and Jones. The first story opens in dialogue. A narrator walks an engaged girl away from a party and teases her that everyone else seems afraid of an engaged girl, while he is made of sterner stuff.

He wants the whole story of her engagement to Gerard Malcolm: what each of them found to like, and what the Englishman said. She answers that he has no claim to read that sealed book. Banter turns confessional as he reminds her he was the first person to love her, and she retorts that he was conceited, jealous, and exacting while it lasted.
the-principles-of-aesthetics: DeWitt H. Parker, professor of philosophy at the University of Michigan, opens The Principles of Aesthetics with a preface. The book grew out of his lectures, and he aimed at scientific accuracy with freedom of style. His heaviest debts, he says, run to Herder through Hegel, and among contemporaries to Croce and Lipps. Contents begin with a definition of art and the analysis of the aesthetic experience. The pages provided hold the preface and contents heads only, not the chapters.
under-the-lilacs: Louisa May Alcott wrote Under the Lilacs, a story for young readers. She signed the dedication to four children she calls her new friends and sisters overseas. Only the contents list and the first lines of chapter one are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The contents run to twenty-four chapters. They promise a stray dog, a boy named Ben who finds a place, a happy tea, a runaway, and a birthday. The opening lines set the scene on an elm-lined avenue.
